content: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have provided detailed guidelines for the cleaning, disinfection, and disposal of medical devices and equipment, particularly in high-risk settings such as Ebola care facilities. Below is a professional summary of the procedures and recommendations: General Guidelines for Medical Devices 1. Hospital-Acquired Infection Prevention: WHO emphasizes the importance of cleaning and disinfecting medical devices to prevent hospital-acquired infections. Devices such as stethoscopes, sphygmomanometers, pulse oximeters, and infrared thermometers must be decontaminated using alcohol (70% isopropyl or ethanol) or chlorine-based solutions. Alcohol solutions should be replaced weekly, while chlorine solutions may corrode stainless steel and reduce device lifespan. 2. Device-Specific Cleaning: Stethoscopes: Disassemble into ear tips, ear tubes, plastic tubing, and chest piece. Remove the diaphragm for cleaning if possible. Sphygmomanometers: Separate the cuff from the manometer. Do not disassemble the manometer. Pulse Oximeters: Disassemble into monitor, cable, lens, detector, and probe. Remove batteries if battery-operated. Infrared Thermometers: Disassemble for cleaning and remove batteries if applicable. 3. Cleaning Procedure: Use a paper towel moistened with disinfectant solution to wipe all surfaces of the device. Hold the towel against each surface for 30 seconds. Avoid immersing devices in the solution. Discard used paper towels in waste designated for incineration. If cloths are used, incinerate them. Allow device parts to air dry in a decontaminated area. Sphygmomanometer cuffs may be cleaned with low-temperature steam if available. 4. Maintenance: Regularly check sphygmomanometers for air leaks or damage to the manometer to prevent mercury loss. Respiratory and Anesthesia Equipment 1. Oxygen Concentrators: Single-use components such as flow splitters, patient masks, and tubing should be cleaned with warm water and detergent during use and discarded afterward. 2. Suction Systems: Suction bottles are single-use and highly infectious. Dispose of them in infectious waste bags for incineration or deep burial. 3. Anesthesia Machines: Follow manufacturer instructions for cleaning and decontamination. Wash dismantled parts with detergent to remove contaminants, rinse, and dry. Avoid water temperatures exceeding 45°C to prevent damage. Single-Use Devices 1. Non-Sharp Devices: Dispose of single-use devices made of polymers in sturdy, clearly labeled bags marked as highly infectious. Final disposal should involve incineration or deep burial. 2. Sharp Devices: Examples include syringes, needles, and intravenous infusion systems. These must be immediately placed in puncture-resistant, fluid-impermeable sharps containers after use. Dispose of containers through incineration or deep burial. Decontamination of Medical Instruments 1. Manual Cleaning: Submerge instruments in cold water (<40°C) with detergent immediately after use to remove debris. Flush instruments with lumens using a water-filled syringe to prevent drying of contaminants. Avoid using hot water or fixation detergents, as these may cause blood contaminants to adhere to the instrument. Rinse with clean water and air dry after soaking and brushing. 2. Disinfection: Use IPC-recommended disinfectant solutions for pathogen deactivation. Avoid exposing electrical components to disinfectants. Waste Management and Facility Decommissioning 1. Reusable Items: Items such as bed frames, stretchers, and tents can be reused if intact and properly decontaminated. Damaged items should be incinerated or sent to a landfill. Wooden shelves and office furniture in low-risk zones can be reused after decontamination and sun drying. 2. Non-Reusable Items: Items such as mattresses with damaged plastic covers, cleaning materials (mops, buckets, brushes), and tents made of absorbable materials should be incinerated. 3. Pits and Trenches: Sharps pits should be capped with concrete and backfilled when less than two-thirds full. Ash pits and organic pits should be backfilled and compacted. Mark these areas for future reference. 4. Water Tanks and Pipes: Decontaminate water tanks and pipes according to SOPs. Reuse if intact; otherwise, dispose of them appropriately. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Full PPE must be worn in high-risk zones during decontamination processes. Lower-level PPE is sufficient in green zones for handling cleaned and disinfected items. Final Disposal and Redistribution Items that cannot be reused should be incinerated or buried deeply. Reusable items in good condition can be redistributed to other healthcare facilities after proper sterilization.
